plan: [This is a 5-bidder, third-price sealed-bid auction. In the symmetric Bayes–Nash equilibrium the bidding function is b(v) = (n-1)/(n-k+1) * v = 4/3 v, which balances winning probability versus paying the third-highest bid. With my private value v = 36 this gives b = 48.00. I will submit $48.00 (allowed in $0.1 increments) to maximize expected profit under symmetric play; no prior rounds to update strategies.]

[My value (8) is well below the expected third-highest order statistic (~24.5 for five uniform [0,49] players), so bidding aggressively risks large negative payoff. With independent draws and a single round, the safest long-run-maximizing move is to avoid winning when value is low. I will bid the minimum to minimize chance of overpaying and preserve profit.]

[I will bid my true private value, $44. With a third-price rule and independent uniform values, bidding up to your value increases win probability without increasing the price you pay (the third-highest bid). With no prior history and a high value near the top of the distribution, truthful bidding maximizes expected surplus while avoiding overbidding risk. I'll submit $44.0 to respect $0.1 increments.]

[There are 4 opponents. In a 3rd‑price auction with symmetric strategies, the price when I win equals the 2nd‑highest of the 4 opponents. Condition on my value v being the highest; opponents are i.i.d. Uniform[0,v]. The expected 2nd‑highest of 4 opponents is (3/5)v = 0.6v. Bidding b(v)=0.6v is the symmetric Bayes‑Nash equilibrium/heuristic here. With v=32, bid 0.6*32=19.2 to maximize long‑run expected profit.]

[I model opponents as symmetric with values uniform on [0,49]. For a third-price auction with 5 bidders the symmetric Bayes–Nash equilibrium is linear. Solving the first-order condition for best response (maximize win prob * surplus) gives b(v) = (4/3) v. With my private value $24 the equilibrium bid is (4/3)*24 = $32. I will bid that to maximize expected long-run profit.]
